name: Phalaris

project_scope.scope: Existing canonical species only; no new admission

look_here_first: CAROLINA CANARYGRASS (maygrass): look for a fairly firm, dense, oval-to-elongate light-green head with overlapping pointed, faintly green-and-pale-striped glumes, above flat shiny leaves on an ANNUAL grass. The true test is ONE dissected 4–6 mm spikelet: two narrow, hairy REDUCED STERILE florets below one fertile floret, surrounded by two keeled, narrowly winged glumes. Introduced lesser canarygrass (Phalaris minor) has ONE reduced sterile floret; head shape, flowering color and site moisture are insufficient by themselves. Five new physical Bob Harms photographs now lead from whole plant to compact panicle, overlapping spikelets and sheath/collar. No true drawn diagram or source image resolves individually labeled two sterile florets; crew needs a real dissected source-vouchered measured floret.

recognition.where_to_look_first: CAROLINA CANARYGRASS (maygrass): look for a fairly firm, dense, oval-to-elongate light-green head with overlapping pointed, faintly green-and-pale-striped glumes, above flat shiny leaves on an ANNUAL grass. The true test is ONE dissected 4–6 mm spikelet: two narrow, hairy REDUCED STERILE florets below one fertile floret, surrounded by two keeled, narrowly winged glumes. Introduced lesser canarygrass (Phalaris minor) has ONE reduced sterile floret; head shape, flowering color and site moisture are insufficient by themselves.
priority: Full rooted spring grass with fibrous annual roots, multiple leafy culms, intact seedhead and an actual ruler
Same-shoot leaf sheath/blade junction showing pale membranous ligule measured with 1-mm scale
One mature detached and OPENED Phalaris caroliniana spikelet, both lateral sides, individually labeled two narrow sterile lemmas and fertile floret with scale
Compare to a confirmed P. minor spikelet with exactly ONE sterile lemma and toothed/erose glume wing in matching magnification
Mat-like fluffy Polypogon monspeliensis foxtail head, with visible awns contrasted against the layered Phalaris head (no false counts from distant photographs)

comparison_lesson.title: Native maygrass vs introduced look-alike canarygrasses
comparison_lesson.memory_rule: CAROLINA: TWO reduced sterile florets + one fertile inside paired keeled glumes. MINOR: ONE reduced sterile floret. The green dense head is a clue, NOT confirmation.
quick_split: Carolina P. caroliniana versus lesser canarygrass P. minor: 2 versus 1 reduced sterile FLORETS below the fertile floret; green compact panicle is shared.
Carolina versus P. canariensis: both have 2 sterile florets but canariensis has broader conspicuous glume wings and larger glumes; visually inspect mature spikelets.
Carolina versus P. angusta: reduced sterile floret lengths and narrow cylindrical head vs Carolina ovoid-lanceolate, with overlap and need for measured comparison.
Carolina versus Polypogon monspeliensis: compact firm keeled glumes versus distinct feathery awns creating a soft bottlebrush.
Carolina versus P. arundinacea: root annual fibrous vs perennial spreading rhizomes, and expanded panicle when flowering.
comparison_lesson.guardrail: Only P. caroliniana installed canonical; other taxa clearly labelled comparisons only; source photo alone does not determine native status or authorize treatment.

comparison_matrix.title: Phalaris — measure sterile florets, not just head shape
rows: Annual, compact layered green head, paler glume wings, usually ovoid-elongate
2 sterile florets (~1.5–2.5 mm), 1 fertile; narrower, generally entire glume wings
Very similar compact green head; often blunt/truncate base
Usually 1 sterile floret (~0.7–1.8 mm); glume wing often toothed/erose
2 sterile florets but broad winged glumes usually 7–10 mm
2 small sterile florets often ~0.7–1.5 mm vs longer Carolina
Rhizomatous perennial root base; do not judge source native lineage
Awned, delicate head instead of paired strongly keeled canarygrass glumes

what_to_teach_crew: At first glance look for a tight green, firm, rather ovoid canarygrass seedhead with sharp overlapping glumes instead of the longer fluffy awn-bearing bottlebrush of Polypogon.
Locate the entire plant base and collar: Carolina canarygrass is a cool-season annual with a membranous ligule; season and damp site are supporting, not decisive.
Separate P. minor from P. caroliniana at magnification by counting reduced STERILE FLORETS inside ONE opened spikelet: ONE in introduced P. minor versus TWO in Carolina canarygrass.
Check P. canariensis: another introduced annual with TWO sterile florets but considerably broader conspicuous glume wings and often larger glumes; do not confuse broad wing with the sterile lemmas.

Check narrow panicles against native P. angusta (two shorter reduced florets, generally narrower cylindrical panicle) and rhizomatous perennial P. arundinacea; both require site/range verification and dissection.
Do not reclassify unknown canarygrass as native based on one photo, nor change Hays county nativity metrics.
visual_needs: LOCAL one isolated mature P. caroliniana spikelet with two reduced sterile florets distinguishable and labeled at 1-mm scale
SAME MAGNIFICATION P. minor spikelet showing its single reduced sterile floret (not a second Carolina card)
Measured true ligule and fibrous annual root of the SAME Carolina canarygrass specimen
P. angusta narrower-headed comparison with independently verified species determination

items.label: Carolina canarygrass — real source photo
items.image_role: Existing physically present species-labelled JPEG visually inspected; only gross structure markers certified
items.caption: Existing CC BY-NC photograph of a compact green Carolina canarygrass flowering head. Two earlier gross-feature arrows show its firm spikelike panicle and overlapping green scales. A single outer scale cannot be called one entire floret; reduced sterile florets and ligule are NOT resolved here. This is an existing source determination, not a microscopic species voucher.
items.why_it_matters: Recognize the firm, overlapping, often pale-striped keeled-glume head; then contrast with the visually very similar introduced lesser canarygrass and count real sterile florets.
items.creator: Andy Newman
items.photo_status: Original physically archived iNaturalist CC BY-NC source photo preserved with TWO previously inspected gross-feature arrows; not proof of inner spikelet anatomy.

items.label: CAROLINA CANARYGRASS — a fresh flowering head framed by real leaf blades

items.caption: A small, tight, pointed green canarygrass panicle stands above broad-to-narrow, flat grass leaves. Learn its firm densely overlapped head and surrounding leaf context. Not a photograph of an individual dissected spikelet, and the two sterile florets cannot be counted here.

items.label: DIFFERENT SPECIES — Phalaris minor head with overlapping pointed glumes
items.image_role: True source-labelled, publicly CC BY licensed Phalaris minor flowering-head comparison from Australia. NOT Carolina canarygrass and not a Texas specimen.
items.caption: This introduced lesser canarygrass ALSO makes a dense, green, layered canarygrass head and can expose dark-purple anthers. The similarity is the lesson: dissect an actual individual spikelet before using this as P. caroliniana. Lesser canarygrass generally has ONE sterile floret, Carolina TWO; that diagnostic difference is NOT visible in this full-head photograph.
items.why_it_matters: Stops the crew from claiming every green pointed canarygrass head is native maygrass; the verified species-level key is the reduced sterile-floret count, not anther color.
items.creator: Harry Rose (Macleay Grass Man)
items.modification_note: Original image pixels unchanged; arrows are HTML overlays only.
items.photo_status: 2026-10-21 Wikimedia Commons confirmed this exact photograph by Harry Rose licensed CC BY 2.0 and its 960px preview viewed; two arrows to visibly real seedhead and protruding anthers only. Reference image, DIFFERENT SPECIES; not a P. caroliniana photo or sterile-floret micro-key.

items.caption: STUDY PHOTO OF REED CANARYGRASS — NOT CAROLINA CANARYGRASS. Follow the original printed abbreviations: Glu = paired glumes; Lem′ and Lem″ = first and second reduced sterile lemmas; Lem‴ = fertile lemma; Pal = palea. Real original 5-mm scale shown. Use this to understand where to look while dissecting a mature P. caroliniana spikelet; it cannot supply a species-specific sterile-lemma count or measurements.
